Players have scored more than 3,000 goals<ref>{{cite web |url=https://inside.fifa.com/data-centre/matches?competitionClassificationCode=FWC |title=International match archive |website=FIFA.com |access-date=6 July 2026}}</ref> in the 23 men's [[FIFA World Cup]] tournaments, the goal record includes [[own goal|own goals]] scored, but  not counting [[List of FIFA World Cup penalty shoot-outs|penalty shoot-outs]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Second-half surge sees Tunisia bow out in style |url=https://www.fifa.com/worldcup/news/second-half-surge-sees-tunisia-bow-out-in-style |publisher=FIFA |access-date=9 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180628222456/https://www.fifa.com/worldcup/news/second-half-surge-sees-tunisia-bow-out-in-style |archive-date=28 June 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref> Since the first goal, by [[France national football team|French]] player [[Lucien Laurent]] in [[1930 FIFA World Cup|1930]],<ref name=milestones>{{cite report |date=October 2007 |url=https://www.fifa.com/mm/document/fifafacts/mcwc/ip-301_02a_fwc_goals_22689.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081203015017/http://www.fifa.com/mm/document/fifafacts/mcwc/ip-301_02a_fwc_goals_22689.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=3 December 2008 |title=FIFA World Cup — Milestone Goals |publisher=FIFA |page=1 |access-date=5 September 2014}}</ref> nearly 1,300 <!-- 1,298 --> footballers have scored goals at the World Cup tournaments,<ref name=worldfootball />{{Update inline|date=July 2026}} of whom 111 have scored five or more.

The top goalscorer of the inaugural competition was [[Argentina national football team|Argentina]]'s [[Guillermo Stábile]], with eight goals. Since then, only 28 players have scored more World Cup goals in total than Stábile did during the 1930 tournament. The first to do so was [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]]'s [[Ademir de Menezes|Ademir]] in [[1950 FIFA World Cup|1950]], with nine goals. This was followed by [[Hungary national football team|Hungary]]'s [[Sándor Kocsis]] scoring eleven in [[1954 FIFA World Cup|1954]]. At the [[1958 FIFA World Cup|1958 tournament]], France's [[Just Fontaine]] further improved on this record, recording thirteen goals in just six matches. [[Gerd Müller]] then scored ten goals for [[Germany national football team|West Germany]] in [[1970 FIFA World Cup|1970]], before breaking the overall record when he scored his fourteenth World Cup goal during West Germany's win in the [[1974 FIFA World Cup final|1974 final]]. Müller's record stood for more than three decades, until [[Ronaldo (Brazilian footballer)|Ronaldo]] recorded fifteen goals between [[1998 FIFA World Cup|1998]] and [[2006 FIFA World Cup|2006]] for Brazil. Germany's [[Miroslav Klose]] broke Ronaldo's record with his 16th goal in [[2014 FIFA World Cup|2014]]; his record stood until Argentina's [[Lionel Messi]] scored his 17th through 21st goals in [[2026 FIFA World Cup|2026]]. At the same World Cup, France's [[Kylian Mbappé]] became the current record holder after scoring his 22nd goal.

Of all the players who have played at the World Cup, only six have achieved an average of two goals or more per match played: Kocsis, Fontaine, Stábile, [[Russia national football team|Russia]]'s [[Oleg Salenko]], [[Switzerland national football team|Switzerland]]'s [[Josef Hügi]], and [[Poland national football team|Poland]]'s [[Ernst Wilimowski]]{{nbsp}}– the latter of whom scored four in his [[Brazil v Poland (1938 FIFA World Cup)|only ever World Cup match]], played in 1938.<ref name=goalscorers>{{cite web |url=https://www.fifa.com/fifa-tournaments/statistics-and-records/worldcup/players/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150828021632/http://www.fifa.com/fifa-tournaments/statistics-and-records/worldcup/players/index.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=28 August 2015 |title=FIFA World Cup Players Statistics |publisher=FIFA |date=25 July 2014 |access-date=30 July 2014}}</ref> The top 111 goalscorers have represented 31 nations, with 15 players scoring for both Brazil and Germany or West Germany. In total, 75 footballers came from [[UEFA]] (Europe), 31 from [[CONMEBOL]] (South America), and only five from elsewhere: [[Cameroon national football team|Cameroon]], [[Ghana national football team|Ghana]] and [[Senegal national football team|Senegal]] from [[Confederation of African Football|CAF]] (Africa), [[Australia men's national soccer team|Australia]] from [[Asian Football Confederation|AFC]] (Asia) (formerly from [[Oceania Football Confederation|OFC]] of Oceania), and the [[United States men's national soccer team|United States]] from [[CONCACAF]] (North/Central America).

Fontaine's thirteen goals in 1958 remains the record for the most scored in a single World Cup tournament. The players that came closest to this tally were Kocsis in 1954 (eleven goals), Müller in 1970 (ten goals), Mbappé in 2026 (ten goals), Brazil's Ademir in 1950 (nine goals) and [[Portugal national football team|Portugal]]'s [[Eusébio]] in [[1966 FIFA World Cup|1966]] (nine goals). The top scorers with the fewest goals were from the [[1962 FIFA World Cup|1962 tournament]], when six players finished joint-top with four goals each. Across the 23 tournaments of the World Cup, 31 footballers have been credited as the tournament top scorer; Mbappé is the only player to achieve this feat twice, in [[2022 FIFA World Cup|2022]] and 2026. Ten of these players scored at least seven goals in a tournament, while Brazil's [[Jairzinho]] in 1970, Argentina's Lionel Messi in 2022 and 2026, and [[England national football team|England]]'s [[Jude Bellingham]] and [[Norway national football team|Norway]]'s [[Erling Haaland]] in 2026 were the only footballers to record at least seven goals but still not finish as the tournament's top scorer. These 31 top goalscorers played for 19 nations, with the most (five) coming from Brazil. Another five came from other South American countries, with the remaining 21 coming from Europe.

Brazil's [[Leônidas (footballer, born 1913)|Leônidas]] became the first player to score eight goals in knockout matches across his [[1934 FIFA World Cup|1934]] and [[1938 FIFA World Cup|1938]] World Cup appearances, a feat that was surpassed by Mbappé in 2026 with a total of twelve (including eight from the previous [[2018 FIFA World Cup|2018]] and 2022 tournaments).<ref name="MostKnockoutGoals">{{Cite web |title=Players with most World Cup knockout-phase goals |url=https://www.fifa.com/en/tournaments/mens/worldcup/canadamexicousa2026/articles/players-most-goals-knockout-phase-stage |access-date=2026-07-19 |publisher=FIFA|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260719120815/https://www.fifa.com/en/tournaments/mens/worldcup/canadamexicousa2026/articles/players-most-goals-knockout-phase-stage|archive-date=2026-07-19|url-status=live}}</ref> Mbappé became the first player to score four goals in [[List of FIFA World Cup finals|World Cup final matches]]: he netted one in the [[2018 FIFA World Cup final|2018 final]] followed by a [[Hat-trick#Association football|hat-trick]] in the [[2022 FIFA World Cup final|2022 final]]. England's [[Geoff Hurst]] is the only other player to record a hat-trick in a World Cup final, doing so in [[1966 FIFA World Cup final|1966]].

<gallery mode="packed" heights="230px">
Stabile hurac 1926.jpg | [[Guillermo Stábile]] scored a then-record eight goals for Argentina at the 1930 World Cup.
Leonidas dasilva.jpg | [[Leônidas (footballer, born 1913)|Leônidas]] scored a record eight World Cup goals for Brazil across the 1934 and 1938 tournaments, all of them in knockout matches—a record that stood until 2026.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=Globo Esporte |title=Mbappé passa Leônidas e Ronaldo Fenômeno e se torna o maior artilheiro em mata-matas da Copa |url=https://ge.globo.com/futebol/copa-do-mundo/noticia/2026/06/30/mbappe-passa-leonidas-e-ronaldo-fenomeno-e-se-torna-o-maior-artilheiro-em-mata-matas-de-copas.ghtml |website=Globoesporte |date=30 June 2026 |access-date=7 July 2026 |language=pt}}</ref>
Ademir de Menezes.jpg | [[Ademir de Menezes|Ademir]] scored a record nine World Cup goals for Brazil, all coming at the 1950 tournament.
Sándor Kocsis 1960 cropped.jpg | [[Sándor Kocsis]] was the first player to score ten or more goals in a single World Cup: he scored a record eleven goals in just five matches for Hungary during the 1954 tournament.
Just Fontaine en 1958.jpg | [[Just Fontaine]] scored a record thirteen World Cup goals for France, all coming at the 1958 tournament.
Gerd Müller c1973 (cropped).jpg | [[Gerd Müller]] scored ten goals for West Germany at the 1970 World Cup, and was top goalscorer from 1974 to 2006.
Ronaldo 2002 cropped.jpg | [[Ronaldo (Brazilian footballer)|Ronaldo]] was top goal scorer from 2006 to 2014, scoring fifteen goals for Brazil, including two in the [[2002 FIFA World Cup final|2002 final]].
2016209185719 2016-07-27 Champions for Charity - Sven - 1D X - 0149 - DV3P4742 mod.jpg | Scoring 16 goals for Germany, [[Miroslav Klose]] was top goalscorer from 2014 to 2026.
Lionel Messi Argentina v Egypt 7 July 2026-112(cropped).jpg | [[Lionel Messi]] was the first player to score twenty goals.
Kylian Mbappe France v Senegal 16 June 2026-391 (cropped).jpg | [[Kylian Mbappé]] holds the record at 22 goals.
</gallery>

== Goalscorers at multiple tournaments ==

Portugal's [[Cristiano Ronaldo]] is the only player to have scored in six World Cups, while Argentina's [[Lionel Messi]] has scored in five. Five players ([[Uwe Seeler]], [[Pelé]], [[Miroslav Klose]], [[Ivan Perišić]] and [[Neymar]]) have each scored in four tournaments, while another 39 have each scored in three.

In the table below players with the same rank are listed in order of achieving their tally.

== Top goalscorers in knockout matches ==
The format has varied considerably between different tournaments, resulting in different numbers of knockout matches per tournament. The 1934 and 1938 World Cups were exclusively knockout competitions. The 1950 edition featured no knockout games, as the champion was decided by a final group stage. Four others had very few: 1930 (three), 1974 (two), 1978 (two) and 1982 (four):<ref name="MostKnockoutGoals" />

* The 1930 tournament featured only three knockout matches after the group stage, consisting of the two semi-finals and the final.
* In 1974 and 1978, a second group phase replaced the traditional quarter-finals and semi-finals used from 1954 through 1970, leaving only the final and third-place match as knockout fixtures.
* The 1982 tournament featured four knockout matches, consisting of the reintroduced semi-final stage alongside the third-place match and final. It also marked the last time a second group phase was used instead of direct knockout rounds after the group stage.
